{{Short description|Rediscovery of the trapezoidal rule in 1994}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=May 2025}}
{{Dark mode invert|[[File:Trapezium2.gif|right|thumb|An animation showing how the [[trapezoidal rule]] approximation improves with more divisions.]]}}
In 1994, [[Nutritional science|nutrition scholar]] Mary M. Tai published a paper in the journal ''[[Diabetes Care]]'' entitled "'''A Mathematical Model for the Determination of Total Area Under Glucose Tolerance and Other Metabolic Curves'''". In the paper, Tai proposes "'''Tai's model'''" as a method of estimating the area under a curve by dividing the area into simple polygons and summing their totals.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Tai |first=Mary M. |title=A Mathematical Model for the Determination of Total Area Under Glucose Tolerance and Other Metabolic Curves |journal=Diabetes Care |date=1994 |volume=17 |issue=2 |pages=152–154 |doi=10.2337/diacare.17.2.152 |pmid=8137688 }}</ref> Apparently unbeknownst to Tai, and not noted by [[Scholarly peer review|peer reviewers]] or the journal's editors, her method is in fact the [[trapezoidal rule]],<ref name=felton>{{Cite web |date=2025-03-11 |title=In 1994, A Paper Claimed To Invent A Key Mathematical Rule Established Centuries Ago |url=https://www.iflscience.com/in-1994-a-paper-claimed-to-invent-a-key-mathematical-rule-established-centuries-ago-78368 |access-date=2025-05-05 |last=Felton |first=James |website=IFL Science }}</ref> a basic method of [[calculus]] used by [[Babylonian astronomy|Babylonian astronomers]] before 50 BCE and later independently by English and French astronomers in the 14th century.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Ancient Babylonian astronomers calculated Jupiter's position from the area under a time-velocity graph |last=Ossendrijver |first=Mathieu |journal=Science |date=2016 |volume=351 |number=6272 |pages=482–484 |doi=10.1126/science.aad8085 }}</ref><ref name=orlin>{{Cite book |last=Orlin |first=Ben |title=Change is the only constant: the wisdom of calculus in a madcap world |date=2019 |publisher=Black Dog & Leventhal Publishers |isbn=978-0-316-50908-4 |edition= |location=New York |chapter=XXII. 1994, The Year Calculus was Born}}</ref>

Several scholars replied to the paper in letters to the journal, objecting to the naming of "Tai's model" and the treatment of a method "used in undergraduate calculus courses" as a novel discovery in the field of [[diabetes]] care.<ref name=bender>{{cite journal |last=Bender |first1=Ralf |title=Determination of the Area Under a Curve |journal=Diabetes Care |date=1994 |volume=17 |issue=10 |department=Letters |pages=1223 |doi=10.2337/diacare.17.10.1223a |pmid=7821150 }}</ref><ref name=wolever>{{cite journal |last=Wolever |first1=Thomas M. S. |title= Comments on Tai's Mathematic Model |journal=Diabetes Care |date=1994 |volume=17 |issue=10 |department=Letters |pages=1223–1224 |doi=10.2337/diacare.17.10.1233b |pmid=7821151 }}</ref><ref name=monaco>{{Cite journal |last1=Monaco |first1=Jane |last2=Anderson |first2=Randy |date=1994 |title=Tai's Formula Is the Trapezoidal Rule |journal=Diabetes Care |department=Letters |volume=17 |issue=10 |pages=1224–1225 |doi=10.2337/diacare.17.10.1224 |pmid=7677819 }}</ref><ref name=shannon>{{cite journal |last1=Shannon |first1=A. G. |last2=Owen |first2=D. R. |title=Modeling Metabolic Curves |journal=Diabetes Care |date=1994 |volume=17 |issue=10 |department=Letters |pages=1225 |doi=10.2337/diacare.17.10.1225a |pmid=7821152 }}</ref> A letter entitled "Tai's Formula is the Trapezoidal Rule" pointed out errors in Tai's representation of the underlying mathematics (such as referring to a count of square units below the curve as the "true value" of the area, against which to measure the accuracy of Tai's model) and problems with the method's applicability to glucose tolerance curves, which are already approximations.{{r|monaco}}<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Allison |first1=David B |last2=Paultre |first2=Furcy |last3=Maggio |first3=Carol |last4=Mezzitis |first4=Nicholas |last5=Pi-Sunyer |first5=F Xavier |date=1995 |title=The Use of Areas Under Curves in Diabetes Research |journal=Diabetes Care |volume=18 |issue=2 |pages=245–250 |doi=10.2337/diacare.18.2.245 |pmid=7729306 }}</ref>

Tai responded, saying that she had derived the method independently during a session with her statistical advisor in 1981, and noting that "the concept behind it is obviously common sense".<ref name="tai reply">{{Cite journal |last=Tai |first=Mary M. |date=1994 |title=Reply From Mary Tai |journal=Diabetes Care |volume=17 |issue=10 |department=Letters |pages=1225–1226 |doi=10.2337/diacare.17.10.1225b }}</ref> She explained that she submitted her method for publication at the request of her colleagues at the Obesity Research Center, who had already been using it in their own work under the name "Tai's formula" and wanted to cite a formal source.{{r|tai reply}} Tai argues that her contribution "presented the original concept into a functioning mathematical description that can be easily observed and applied".{{r|tai reply}} Mathematicians [[Stephan Ramon Garcia|Stephan Garcia]] and [[Steven J. Miller|Steven Miller]] retort that "every calculus book in existence presents the trapezoidal rule in a manner that can easily be applied!"<ref name=garcia>{{Cite book |last=Garcia |first=Stephan Ramon |title=100 years of math milestones: the Pi Mu Epsilon centennial collection |last2=Miller |first2=Steven J. |date=2019 |publisher=American Mathematical Society |isbn=978-1-4704-3652-0 |series=AMS Non-Series Monographs |location=Providence, Rhode Island |pages=435–436}}</ref>

Tai's 1994 paper has been cited over 500 times as of March 2025. The episode has been cited as an illustration of the slower-than-expected spread of knowledge in certain contexts.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Arbesman |first=Samuel |title=The Half-Life of Facts: Why Everything We Know Has an Expiration Date |date=27 August 2013 |publisher=[[Penguin Publishing Group]] |isbn=978-1591846512 |pages=63–64}}</ref> Garcia and Miller call it a cautionary tale in verifying the originality of one's work before publishing it.{{r|garcia}} Author Ben Orlin cautions against contemptuous judgment of someone trying to share what they had learned, and criticizes academic publishing's focus on credit and lack of venues for small contributions.{{r|orlin}}
